data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Decentralized networks are more vulnerable to the exact class of correlated failures they are advertised as solving, because they cannot enforce or verify the independence they rely on. The apparent uncorrelatedness of small operators is an epistemological artifact of small samples and short observation windows; a large service can engineer and test independence of its redundancy, while a decentralized network cannot even measure it.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If a decentralized network had strong empirical evidence of long-run uncorrelated failure modes across its operators (e.g., a multi-year dataset showing no coincident failures across unrelated operators), the claim would weaken.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If large services were shown to have a poor historical record of actually verifying independence (e.g., widespread simultaneous failures of redundant components within large services), the claim would weaken.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The large service has a closed dependency graph for its redundancy: it can enumerate the components, test for shared dependencies, and actively inject faults to verify isolation. A decentralized network has an open dependency graph: operators independently choose software, hardware, and upstream providers. The network cannot observe or control these choices, so it cannot detect hidden common dependencies (e.g., all operators happen to rely on the same cloud provider, the same TLS library, or the same upstream transit). The very autonomy that is claimed as resilience is the mechanism that prevents the detection of correlated risk.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
